claims.statement: Five hundred thousand dollars a year. For a rookie who had never played a single NBA game.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013: 'Nike offered Jordan $500,000 a year in cash for five years'. The pitch happened after the summer 1984 Olympics. Wikipedia gives the signing as Oct 26, 1984, the day of his NBA debut, so the offer came before any NBA game (N1 confirmed).

claims.statement: About three times the best shoe deal around / Nike is about to smash the record.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013: 'The previous highest contract was James Worthy's deal with New Balance, an eight-year deal worth $150,000 a year.' Wikipedia: 'three times more than any other deal in the NBA at the time.'

claims.statement: From a company that had just lost money / Nike posted its first quarterly loss. Ever. (February)
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013: 'In February 1984, the company reported its first quarterly loss ever.'

claims.statement: Under thirty million in sales in 1973; $867M by the end of '83; yearly sales about $867M.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013: 'revenue went from $28.7 million in 1973 to $867 million by the end of 1983.'

claims.statement: It's been a public company since 1980.
claims.evidence: Knight, 2004 letter: 'When we went public in 1980, we had 7,500 original investors.'

claims.statement: Even in its rough year, Nike still made over forty million in profit.
claims.evidence: Knight quoting his 1984 letter: 'In fiscal year 1984, we made over $40 million in net income, which represents a 16 percent return on equity.'

claims.statement: A rival called Reebok is coming up fast / by the mid-eighties Reebok passed Nike as America's biggest athletic shoe maker; by 1988 it had lost that top spot.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (citing WSJ 2005): sales $13M in 1983; 'By mid-decade, Reebok's sales were about $1 billion, and it overtook Nike ... as the largest athletic shoe manufacturer in the US before losing the top position in 1988.'

claims.statement: Since 1977, Vaccaro has signed about eighty college coaches.
claims.evidence: USA Today 2015: 'Vaccaro joined Nike in 1977 ... signing endorsement deals with about 80 coaches.'

claims.statement: College player of the year. The Chicago Bulls take him third in the draft, on June 19.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2016, Falk: 'He was the national player of the year.' 3rd pick on June 19, 1984 is in the research dossier (s10) and is undisputed.

claims.statement: He wore Converse in college. He wanted Adidas. He had never even worn a pair (of Nikes).
claims.evidence: ESPN 2016: 'Jordan wore Converse in college and preferred Adidas.' USA Today 2015, Jordan: 'In all honesty, I never wore Nike shoes until I signed with Nike.'

claims.statement: Phil Knight, co-founder and boss; Rob Strasser, the marketing chief; agent David Falk.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013: 'Nike president and co-founder Phil Knight'. ESPN 2016: '[marketing head] Rob Strasser'. Falk was Jordan's agent.

claims.statement: Converse is offering him about a hundred thousand dollars a year.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013: 'a financial package of about $100,000 a year'. ESPN 2016: 'Converse offered $100,000 per year.'

claims.statement: Five hundred thousand a year. For five years. About two and a half million dollars in cash.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013 and 2016: $500,000 a year for five years. Wikipedia: 'six-year, $2.5 million deal' (length disputed; script follows the majority; the total of about $2.5M is consistent).

claims.statement: Add stock options, and by Falk's count the package could reach about seven million.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013: 'Adding stock options and other parts of the deal, Falk said Jordan would earn $7 million over those five years, as long as Nike didn't sever the contract.' Attributed.

claims.statement: According to ESPN's reporting, Spot-Bilt bid more (Nike's offer wasn't the biggest in cash).
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013: 'In straight-up cash, Spot-Bilt's deal would be worth more than what Nike offered.' ESPN 2016: Spot-Bilt 'submitted the highest bid, including Nike.'

claims.statement: His own shoe line. His name on it. And royalties: a cut of the sales.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: Nike would make him 'a stand alone star and give him a signature shoe line'; 'Jordan would get royalties from products sold by Nike with his name.' Jordan (USA Today) says Strasser presented 'the Air Jordan concept'. ESPN 2013 says Falk came up with the Air Jordan name in the weeks after the deal; 'his name on it' as a description of a signature line is acceptable.

claims.statement: By Falk's account, a million dollars of marketing in the first six months.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013: Falk 'said he made them commit to putting $1 million into marketing Jordan's shoes in their first six months on the shelves.'

claims.statement: Jordan's fee was less than a tenth of one percent of $867M.
According to Falk, an escape hatch: miss Rookie of the Year, All-Star, 20 ppg in his first three years and Nike could walk away two years early.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013: 'if he didn't accomplish one of three things -- win Rookie of the Year, become an All-Star or average 20 points per game -- in his first three years, it could end the deal two years early.' ESPN 2016 gives a $4M sales version; both come from the Falk-sourced reporting. Attribution is adequate.

claims.statement: Jordan didn't want to go. His parents talked him into it.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013: 'I have no interest in going there'; Falk called James and Deloris. Jordan (USA Today): 'my parents made me go out'.

claims.statement: At Nike's HQ in Oregon: highlight tape to the Pointer Sisters' 'Jump'; a shoe built around him; by Falk's telling Strasser pulled out two toy Mercedes cars.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013: Beaverton, Ore.; 'highlight tape of himself to the Pointer Sisters "Jump"'; Moore 'could tailor them to Jordan's liking'; 'Strasser reached in and took out two die-cast Mercedes cars.'

claims.statement: "I was very loyal," he later told ESPN. ... "This is the Nike contract, if you come anywhere close, I'll sign with you guys."
claims.evidence: The quote is verbatim in ESPN 2013, but Rovell introduces it with 'Jordan said at the time', not as something Jordan told ESPN later. The attribution 'later told ESPN' is not supported.
claims.fix: "I was very loyal," Jordan said, as quoted by ESPN.

claims.statement: By Falk's account, Adidas had shown almost no interest. And Adidas didn't come close.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2016 says it in the reporter's own voice ('By all accounts, Adidas had almost no interest in Jordan'), and ESPN 2013 says 'adidas wasn't making an offer' (family turmoil). Neither text attributes this to Falk. 'Didn't come close' is supported ('It wasn't happening').
claims.fix: According to ESPN's reporting, Adidas had shown almost no interest.

claims.statement: That fall, Michael Jordan signed with Nike.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: 'On October 26, 1984, Jordan signed...'. USA Today: deal 'consummated in 1984'. 'That fall' is safely vague.

claims.statement: The NBA banned his red and black Nike shoes. The reported fine: five thousand dollars a game. Nike ... paid.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: '$5,000 fine per game ... Nike agreed to pay each fine.' ESPN 2013: 'Nike paid the fines and made a commercial.' Slate: Granik letter, 'red and black Nike basketball shoes', around Oct 18, 1984; the game shoe was likely the Air Ship. The script's wording follows myth 7.

claims.statement: Ad punchline: "Fortunately, the NBA can't keep you from wearing them."
claims.evidence: Verbatim in ESPN 2013 and Slate 2023.

claims.statement: Air Jordan One hit stores in spring 1985. $65 a pair. Goal: $3M over three years.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013: '$65 a pair, hit stores nationwide in March 1985'. Wikipedia: released April 1985 'with the goal of making $3 million in the first three years.'

claims.statement: By May, seventy million dollars' worth. By the end of the first year, more than a hundred million. More than thirty times the goal, in a third of the time.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013: 'By May, Nike had sold $70 million worth. By year's end ... more than $100 million in revenues.' Wikipedia's $126M is flagged as disputed; the conservative figure is used. $100M / $3M = 33x.

claims.statement: Escape hatch never needed. Jordan was Rookie of the Year. He made the All-Star team.
claims.evidence: ESPN 2013: 'won the Rookie of the Year award'. 1985 All-Star selection per research s10 (undisputed).

claims.statement: In 1997, Jordan became a brand of its own.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: 'In 1997, Jordan and Nike introduced Jordan Brand (originally called "Brand Jordan").'

claims.statement: In 2022 alone, Jordan Brand brought in five point one billion. About two thousand times the whole cash deal.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: 'In 2022 alone, Jordan Brand brought in $5.1 billion to Nike.' $5.1B / $2.5M = 2,040x (about 1,700x if six years at $3M; 'about two thousand' holds).

claims.statement: Today, that bet brings in more than five billion dollars a year.
claims.evidence: Nike FY2026 earnings release (SEC exhibit 99.1), footnote 3: 'sales of Jordan Brand products which were $7,034 million in fiscal 2026 compared to $7,270 million in fiscal 2025.' N2 confirmed.

claims.statement: Jordan's reported Nike earnings that year: $150 to $256 million.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: 'a reported $150–256 million went directly to Jordan under his royalties deal with Nike.' Stated as a reported range.

claims.statement: Nike as a whole: from $867M to $46.4B in fiscal 2026. About fifty times bigger.
claims.evidence: Nike FY2026 release: 'Full year revenues were $46.4 billion' ($46,398M). $46,398M / $867M = 53.5x.

claims.statement: Jordan: "Would the brand have been as strong if it was adidas? We'll never know."
claims.evidence: Verbatim in ESPN 2013.

claims.statement: Vaccaro says he picked Jordan and urged Nike to spend its budget on him. Knight and Jordan dispute his role. The 2023 movie goes further: Nike's whole basketball budget, on one rookie. Our research found no primary source for that.
claims.evidence: USA Today 2015: Vaccaro 'urged Nike to spend all of its allotted budget to sign Jordan.' So 'whole budget on one rookie' IS Vaccaro's own first-hand claim. It is not something only the movie adds, and saying there is 'no primary source' contradicts the previous sentence. What the film adds (Slate) is Vaccaro betting his job and the whole basketball division; the specific $250,000 budget figure has no primary source.
claims.fix: Vaccaro says he picked Jordan and urged Nike to spend its whole allotted budget on him. Knight and Jordan dispute his role. The 2023 movie goes further: Vaccaro bets his job, and the whole basketball division, on one rookie. For that version, we found no source beyond Vaccaro's own account.

claims.statement: Knight credits Strasser and Moore; "Sonny helped, but he wasn't the MVP in that process." Jordan credits Strasser and George Raveling.
claims.evidence: Verbatim in USA Today 2015. Knight: MVPs were Strasser and Moore. Jordan: 'it was actually George Raveling' and 'I absolutely fell in love with (Strasser)'.

claims.statement: Vaccaro was fired by Nike in 1991. Knight: "Success has a thousand fathers and failure is an orphan."
claims.evidence: USA Today 2015: 'fired by Nike in 1991 without public explanation'; Knight quote verbatim.

issues: REVEAL: '"I was very loyal," he later told ESPN.' ESPN 2013 introduces the quote with 'Jordan said at the time', not as a later ESPN interview. Replace with: '"I was very loyal," Jordan said, as quoted by ESPN.' (Keep the rest of the quote; it is verbatim.)

REVEAL: 'By Falk's account, Adidas had shown almost no interest.' In ESPN this is the reporter's own wording ('By all accounts...'), not Falk's. Replace with: 'According to ESPN's reporting, Adidas had shown almost no interest.'

AFTERMATH (credit fight): 'The twenty twenty-three movie goes further: Nike's whole basketball budget, on one rookie. Our research found no primary source for that.' This contradicts the line before it. Vaccaro himself told USA Today he urged Nike to spend 'all of its allotted budget' on Jordan. Replace the passage with: 'Vaccaro says he picked Jordan and urged Nike to spend its whole allotted budget on him. Knight and Jordan dispute his role. The 2023 movie goes further: Vaccaro bets his job, and the whole basketball division, on one rookie. For that version, we found no source beyond Vaccaro's own account.'
notes: The story holds up. All 38 factual statements were checked; 35 are ok. I re-opened ESPN 2013 (s2), ESPN 2016 (s3), USA Today 2015 (s4), Slate 2023 (s5), Wikipedia Air Jordan (s1), Wikipedia Reebok (s11), Knight's 2004 letter (s7), Nike's FY2026 press release (s13) and the FY2026 earnings release on SEC.gov (new primary source for Jordan Brand: $7,034M FY2026, $7,270M FY2025). Open points N1-N6 are resolved: the offer came before his NBA debut; latest Jordan Brand revenue is well above $5B; roles and the Oregon HQ are confirmed by ESPN; five years follows the majority; 'that fall' is safe. Five quotes were checked verbatim (Q1 to Q5); none is disputed or apocryphal; heated and apocryphal quotes are correctly left out. Numbers use the conservative ends (>$100M year one, $5.1B in 2022, the reported $150-256M range), and the ratios (0.058%, 33x, ~2,040x, ~53x) are correct. No inflation-adjusted values are used. Hindsight fairness: strong. The case for walking away comes before the case for signing, and Converse and Adidas are not mocked. Structure: freeze at ~4:23 of ~8:38 (51%), then reveal, numbers, verdict line 'Signed.', one lesson. About 1,290 words at ~150 wpm fits the 8-12 min long format. Optional, not blocking: 'Nike could have backed down. Instead, it paid.' is supported by ESPN and Wikipedia, but Slate shows the ban story is messier (the game shoe was likely the Air Ship). 'Instead, by most accounts, it paid.' would be even safer. All three required fixes are wording-only; no timing impact.
